title: The Bridge of Valparaíso
premise: In 1891 Valparaíso, in the aftermath of Chile's civil war, Noor Zhou, a Chinese-Chilean apprentice clockmaker, is summoned to repair the observatory's master clock and finds hidden inside it the private ledgers of Don Elías Vergara—a customs official officially dead in the fighting, whose meticulous records prove the victors' naval blockade starved the port's poor by design. When a stranger arrives bearing letters in Don Elías's unmistakable hand, Noor realizes the old man is alive, hiding, and counting on someone to carry his truth into print before the government's historians seal the record. Pursued by an officer who once owed Don Elías his life and now owes his career to the lie, Noor must choose between the invisibility that has kept their family safe for two generations and the inheritance of truth left ticking inside the clock. In the end, Noor publishes the ledgers through a foreign shipping gazette, testifies at cost of exile from the trade they love, and winds the master clock one last time—leaving the truth on the record even as the train carries them away.
about_author: August Joubert is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing port records along the Pacific coast before turning to fiction. They write historical novels about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Gears
chapters.summary: Noor Zhou's POV. In their stepfather's cramped workshop above the fish market, Noor is summoned to the Cerro Alegre observatory to repair its master clock—the first commission ever given to a Zhou. Pride wars with the family rule: be precise, be useful, be invisible. The beat is cautious hope, the sense that belonging might finally be within reach.

chapters.title: What the Clock Kept
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Opening the clock's case, Noor finds oilskin-wrapped ledgers documenting blockade shipments and deliberate starvation orders, signed by officials now celebrated as heroes—including the name of the officer who signed the death notice of customs official Don Elías Vergara. The emotional beat is dread disguised as curiosity; some mechanisms, once opened, cannot be closed.

chapters.title: A Stranger with Familiar Ink
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, interrupted by the stranger's account. A gaunt man calling himself Señor Ríos arrives at the workshop carrying letters in Don Elías's handwriting—impossible, since the man is officially dead. He tests Noor with questions about the clock. The beat is vertigo: the ledger is not a relic but a live wire, and someone else knows it exists.

chapters.title: The Officer Who Owes a Debt
chapters.summary: Captain Ignacio Fuenzalida's POV. Fuenzalida, whose career rests on the official version of the war, learns a repairman touched the observatory clock and begins quietly pulling threads through the port's Chinese quarter. Flashbacks reveal Don Elías saved his life at Coquimbo. The beat is corrosive loyalty: gratitude curdling into obligation to a lie.

chapters.title: Lessons in Disappearing
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor's stepfather, Wen, reveals the family's own buried history—papers burned in 1860, names changed at the dock—and forbids contact with Ríos. Noor secretly copies pages of the ledger anyway, hiding them inside clock cases bound for consignment shops. The beat is quiet rebellion; inheritance, Noor realizes, can be refused or claimed.

chapters.title: The Gazette on the Mole
chapters.summary: Noor's POV with Ríos present. Ríos leads Noor to Tomás Iriarte, editor of a foreign shipping gazette beyond Chilean jurisdiction, who agrees to print excerpts—but demands verification and a named source. Meanwhile soldiers search the workshop. The beat is the narrowing of escape routes: truth needs a body willing to stand behind it.

chapters.title: Fire on Cerro Alegre
chapters.summary: Alternating Noor and Fuenzalida POVs. The observatory burns in a fire ruled accidental; the master clock is destroyed, and with it the original ledgers' hiding place—though Noor's copies survive in a pawnshop crate. Fuenzalida realizes too late what he has enabled. The beat is grief and complicity; both protagonists lose the thing that anchored them.

chapters.title: The Dead Man's Testimony
chapters.summary: Ríos's POV, revealed as Don Elías himself. In a hillside safe house, he explains why he faked his death and why he chose Noor: a clockmaker measures time honestly. He offers to surrender himself publicly if Noor will carry the copies to Iriarte. The beat is solemn transfer of weight—an inheritance formally handed over.

chapters.title: Everything That Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Fuenzalida corners Noor at the docks with an offer: silence, protection, a place in the new order. Noor refuses, naming the debt he owes Don Elías aloud, and walks past him to the gazette office as presses roll. The beat is the climax—loyalty finally aligned with truth rather than against it.

chapters.title: Winding the Master Clock
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, epilogue voice. Months later, the gazette's excerpts have forced an inquiry; Don Elías testifies and dies within the year, at peace. Exiled from the guild but employed by Iriarte, Noor boards a northbound ship carrying one salvaged gear from the destroyed clock. The beat is bittersweet resolution: the truth is on the record, and time moves on without asking permission.
